title: Patacara the teacher
hook: the woman who lost everything becomes a teacher of other grieving women

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uppalavanna, foremost in psychic power, who met Mara unafraid. Your line: she survived. Today, a survivor who turned around and taught.

An arrow, lodged where nobody can see it. That's how grieving mothers, in the verses of the elder nuns, speak of their sorrow for their children. And they name the woman who drew it out: Patacara. Tradition tells her losses first: a husband, children, parents, all gone, it says, in a stretch of days so terrible that she wandered out of her mind with grief, until she reached the Buddha. That's usually where the telling stops. Today it keeps going. The woman who lost everything becomes the one other grieving women come looking for.
screen: `AN ARROW NO ONE CAN SEE.` → `SHE DREW IT OUT.` → `THE GRIEVING COME TO HER.`

segments.voice: First, her own waking. In her verses in the Therigatha, Patacara tells how she washed her feet, watched the water run down the slope, and steadied her mind on it. The commentary adds what she saw: some water went a little way, some further, some further still, the way lives run short and long. That evening she took a lamp into her cell, sat on her bed, and drew down the wick with a needle. As the flame went out, her mind was freed. Second, what she says to the grieving. In another poem, mothers remember her words. You don't know the way he came, or the way he went. He came from somewhere unseen and went on somewhere unseen. So why weep, crying, my son? It sounds hard on paper. In the poem it lands as the voice of someone who stood in the same place. Third, what the women say back. She drew the arrow from their hearts, they say, the grief for their children, and they went forth as nuns. Other nuns' verses name her too: they did as Patacara taught, washed their feet, went to their cells, and woke. Fourth, the title. In the list of foremost disciples, Patacara is named first among the nuns who know the discipline, the community's rules. The woman who once wandered wild with grief became the keeper of order. Grief didn't vanish. It became a way to recognize someone else's. From grief to teacher.
screen: `WATER DOWN A SLOPE, A LAMP GOES OUT.` · `HE CAME AND WENT UNSEEN.` · `SHE DREW OUT THE ARROW.` · `KEEPER OF THE DISCIPLINE.` · then, large: `FROM GRIEF TO TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who is grieving now, a loss this year or an old one that still sits close. Patacara didn't lead with answers; she sat with people first, so just keep this person company in your mind, with nothing to fix. Then let them rest there, and come back to your breath.
Salla, a dart or arrow. What grieving women say Patacara drew out of their hearts, the grief for their children. Today's word.
Your line: from grief to teacher. The one who lost everything became the one people came looking for. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Patacara's verses and the verses of the women she taught are read in the Therigatha, and in Theravada communities her story is told as a teaching on grief and on how short and uncertain life is.

chat.says: How did Patacara go from grieving to teaching?
options: She woke, then drew the arrow of grief out of other mothers' hearts.
She forgot her losses entirely, so grief never touched her again.
She stayed away from grieving people so their sorrow couldn't reach her.
chat.meaning: Freed as a lamp went out, Patacara taught grieving mothers, who say she drew the arrow of grief for their children out of their hearts.

notes: All paraphrased; Mrs. Rhys Davids's Psalms of the Sisters (1909) exists, but the writer was not certain of its wording.

Her losses are summarized and attributed to tradition (Dhammapada commentary, verses 113 and 288-289); the count of losses was left out on purpose. Check the hook's 'her own story is the one people tend to tell' reads as fair.

Confirm Thig 6.1 is the poem to grieving mothers ('you don't know the way he came or went') and the 'arrow drawn out' line, and that Thig 5.11 (the thirty nuns, number omitted) follows her instruction about washing feet and entering the cell.
Thig 5.10: confirm she drew down the wick 'with a needle' (pin).

Editor: hook no longer opens on a grieving mother with a dead son (day 760 opens on Kisa Gotami's dead child); it now opens on the arrow image from Thig 6.1, and 'the one people tend to tell' became 'the part tradition tells first'. The water running short, further and further still is from the Dhammapada commentary (v. 113), not her Therigatha verses, so it is now attributed to the commentary. Thig 6.1 is now framed as the mothers remembering her words, and the garbled 'Why cry out, my son?' was fixed.
